meanings.note: Used with para/pra for going back to a place.

examples.text: Vou ter que voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to have to go back to my mother's house.

meanings.note: Links verbs like faltar to an event or destination.
Assumir a liderança and voltar à liderança are standard election-night phrases for taking the lead.

examples.text: Ela voltou à liderança na pesquisa.
examples.trans: She returned to the lead in the poll.

meanings.note: First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?

meanings.note: Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
Used both for the physical sky (céu azul) and in exclamations like Meu Deus do céu! (Good heavens!).
Often reinforced with é que in questions (como é que foi?).

examples.text: Como é que foi a cirurgia?
Como é que tá meu marido?

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Everyday informal Brazilian synonym of colocar or pôr.

examples.text: Na hora de botar de novo, impossível.
examples.trans: When it was time to put it back, impossible.

meanings.note: Grammatically feminine whether referring to a boy, a girl, or children in general.

examples.text: Criança é o futuro do país.
examples.trans: Children are the future of the country.

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.
Also appears in todo mundo (everybody).

examples.text: Como bota criança num mundo desse?
examples.trans: How do you bring a child into a world like this?

meanings.note: Demonstrative determiner; in spoken Brazilian Portuguese esse commonly covers both this near me and that just mentioned.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

examples.text: Vou ficar sentado esse tempo inteiro.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay seated that whole time.

meanings.note: Same singular form for masculine and feminine; plural horríveis.
Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Acabou o seu tempo is the standard phrase for 'Your time is up.'
Contraction of de + aqui.

examples.text: A dor pega daqui até o pescoço.
examples.trans: The pain goes from here up to my neck.

meanings.note: Invariable cardinal number.

examples.trans: I will deposit up to six months.

meanings.note: Calendar month; plural meses drops the circumflex.

examples.trans: I will deposit up to six months.

examples.text: Falta um mês para a viagem.
examples.trans: There is one month left until the trip.

meanings.note: Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
With que it is Brazil's most natural everyday way to say I think / do you think.

examples.text: Eu acho que você tá exagerando.

meanings.note: A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Imperfect devia + infinitive is the everyday spoken way to say should (você devia apagar); present deve + infinitive expresses probability (ele deve ter).

examples.text: Ele deve ter sede lá em Orlando.
examples.trans: He must have a branch there in Orlando.

meanings.note: Used for deleting social media posts or accounts as well as turning off lights.

examples.trans: I am going to delete my app now.

examples.text: Apaga a luz da sala, por favor.
examples.trans: Turn off the room light, please.

meanings.note: Informal second-person singular possessive, very common in Rio speech.

examples.trans: Your husband is already doing great.

meanings.note: English loanword pronounced with final [-tʃi] in Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.text: Você devia apagar teus posts políticos.
examples.trans: You should delete your political posts.

examples.text: Eu vi o seu post hoje.

meanings.note: Follows the noun it modifies: posts políticos (political posts).

examples.text: Você devia apagar teus posts políticos.
examples.trans: You should delete your political posts.

meanings.note: Marks accompaniment or an added ingredient such as sweetener.

examples.text: Ela está com a nossa equipe.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: From chegar (to arrive); com a chegada de means with the arrival of.

examples.text: Com a chegada dos votos, tudo mudou.
examples.trans: With the arrival of the votes, everything changed.

meanings.note: Used for individual ballots and election totals such as votos válidos (valid votes).
With the definite article o nordeste, refers to Brazil's nine-state Northeastern region.

examples.text: O nordeste chegou com muitos votos.
examples.trans: The Northeast arrived with many votes.
We traveled through the Northeast on vacation.

meanings.note: Retomar a liderança means to retake the lead.

examples.text: Lula retoma a liderança no nordeste.
examples.trans: Lula retakes the lead in the Northeast.

meanings.note: Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.
Adds immediacy after imperatives like calma aí, or means there near you.
Used with a or para/pra for reaching a destination.

examples.text: Só pra chegar e comprar um pão.
examples.trans: Just to get there and buy a roll.

explodir.gloss: to blow up; make go viral

meanings.en: to blow up; make go viral
meanings.note: On social media, explodir um vídeo means to make a video blow up / go viral.

examples.trans: Let's make this video blow up!
The news blew up on the internet.

meanings.note: Stress falls on the first syllable; final -deo is pronounced [-dʒju].
Passar impune means to go unpunished; passar por means to undergo.

examples.text: Eles passam por muitos testes lá.
examples.trans: They go through many tests there.

meanings.note: French loanword used across Brazil for New Year's Eve parties and beach celebrations.

examples.text: Vamos passar o réveillon em Salvador.
examples.trans: Let's spend New Year's Eve in Salvador.

examples.text: Onde você vai passar o réveillon?
examples.trans: Where are you going to spend New Year's Eve?

meanings.note: Full form of informal pra; introduces purpose before an infinitive or direction.

examples.trans: I have a lot to sort out.

meanings.note: Takes the preposition em for the place where one lives.

examples.trans: I want to live in a better place.

meanings.note: Points to a place away from the speaker; lá dentro reinforces inside there.
Invariable for gender in the singular: céu azul (blue sky).

examples.text: Lá é céu azul o ano inteiro.
examples.trans: There it is blue sky all year round.

meanings.note: Final -l is vocalized to [w] in Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.text: Lá é céu azul e sol.
examples.trans: There it is blue sky and sunshine.

examples.text: O sol está muito forte hoje.
examples.trans: The sun is very strong today.

meanings.note: Used for hot weather: fazer calor (to be hot outside).

examples.text: Eu adoro o calor do verão.
Que calor que tá fazendo aqui!
examples.trans: What heat it is making here!

meanings.note: Describes both tasty food and pleasant sensations like um calor gostoso (a lovely warmth).

examples.trans: What pleasant warmth at the beach!

meanings.note: Very common in spoken Portuguese for loving things, habits, or activities.
Used figuratively in esse calor move o Brasil (this heat drives Brazil forward).
Everyday friendly farewell across Brazil, borrowed long ago from Italian ciao.
